findings.headline: HRA debt affordability constrained by interest cover ratio of 1.25:1, with £450.2m borrowing planned
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account plans £450.2m borrowing over 2026/27-2029/30 for capital spending. HRA affordability is managed through an agreed interest cover ratio (operating surplus ÷ interest cost) maintained at 1.25:1 minimum, providing limited headroom for rent income variation or cost pressures.
findings.matters: HRA has no Minimum Revenue Provision requirement, so affordability depends entirely on rent income and business plan performance; a 1.25:1 interest cover ratio is tight and leaves no slack for adverse variances.
findings.figures: HRA borrowing 2026/27-2029/30: £450.2m; Interest cover ratio minimum: 1.25:1
findings.quote: The Housing Revenue Account Capital Programme is largely funded from council house rents over time but includes £450.2 million borrowing over the years 2026/27 to 2029/30. The Section 151 Officer has agreed a trajectory of interest cover ratio of 1.25: 1 over the first 4 years of the Business Plan

findings.headline: Reserve balances forecast to decline, eliminating internal borrowing capacity and forcing external market reliance
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly forecasts that reserves and balances will reduce over the short to medium term. The council currently has £102.6m of internal borrowing (using reserve funds to self-fund capital), but this capacity will disappear as reserves deplete.
findings.matters: Loss of reserve cover forces the council into external borrowing markets for all future capital, increasing refinancing risk and exposure to market interest rates.
findings.figures: Current internal borrowing: £102.6m (1 April 2025); average investment balance 2025: £59.1m
findings.quote: Additionally reserves and balances are forecast to reduce over the short to medium term which will lead to reduced balances available for investment or to use for internal borrowing.

findings.headline: Interest payable on debt to rise 84% from £18.2m to £33.4m annually over 4 years
findings.detail: Annual interest costs are forecast to increase from £18.176m in 2026/27 to £33.419m in 2029/30. This reflects the expanded borrowing programme and will crowd out revenue available for council services.
findings.matters: Interest costs are a fixed commitment that reduces budget flexibility; rapid growth signals deteriorating debt serviceability and rising revenue pressure.

findings.headline: External debt to increase nearly threefold from £288.5m to £843.5m over five years
findings.detail: The council plans significant expansion of external borrowing from end 2024/25 to 2029/30, driven by capital programme spending of £489.4m (including £450.2m HRA) and loans to its wholly owned housing company of £45.9m. Prudential borrowing will rise from £509.8m to £999.3m in the same period.
findings.matters: A near-tripling of external debt significantly increases refinancing risk and sensitivity to interest rate movements, constraining future financial flexibility.
findings.figures: External borrowing: £288.5m (end 2024/25) → £843.5m (2029/30); Prudential borrowing: £509.8m → £999.3m; HRA borrowing: £450.2m over 2026/27-2029/30
findings.quote: anticipated external borrowing increasing from £288.5 million at the end of 2024/25 to £843.5 million in 2029/30

findings.headline: Union Street car park income projection at high risk; developer assessment outdated and market conditions weakened
findings.detail: The budget assumes £125k per annum income over four years from the Union Street car park site. This remains a higher risk assumption because the site is constrained, delivery option not yet decided, and the income estimate is based on a developer assessment from several years ago. Officers acknowledge that changing market conditions mean the final figure may be lower.
findings.matters: Another income stream flagged by scrutiny as at-risk, compounding already-identified parking revenue volatility from the congestion charge.
findings.figures: £125k per annum projected income over four years
findings.quote: This remains a higher risk assumption as the site is constrained and the preferred delivery option is not yet decided, with both housing and student accommodation still under consideration. The estimated income figure was based on a developer-led assessment from a number of years ago, and while a financial return is still expected, the changing market conditions mean that final figure may be lower.

findings.headline: ICT spending continues to exceed budget assumptions; legacy contracts and licensing driving overruns
findings.detail: ICT expenditure has continued to exceed earlier assumptions. Key drivers include a legacy data-centre contract from 2016 and Microsoft licensing that has increased approximately 20% year-on-year alongside introduction of new products. Forecasting remains difficult given the number of contracts and pace of supplier pricing changes. Cloud migration introduces continuous revenue costs rather than reducing existing costs.
findings.matters: ICT is a non-discretionary service with cost growth that the council cannot easily control or forecast. Ongoing 20% licensing inflation against a fixed budget is a structural pressure.
findings.figures: Microsoft licensing increases approximately 20% year-on-year
findings.quote: Officers explained that a significant driver remains a legacy data-centre contract Council entered into in 2016, with additional pressures arising from Microsoft licensing, which has seen increases of around 20% year-on-year alongside the introduction of new products and application-specific licences.

findings.headline: Real-terms funding cut: zero cash increase in core spending power despite inflation pressures
findings.detail: The government's provisional three-year local government finance settlement results in cash-terms zero increase in core spending power for Oxford in 2026-27, which represents a real-terms reduction once inflation is taken into account. The settlement is driven primarily by assumed council tax rises rather than new government grant funding.
findings.matters: A real-terms cut to core funding creates structural budget pressure that cannot be resolved through efficiency alone, especially given inflation in pay, contracts and construction costs already built into the budget.
findings.figures: Cash-terms zero increase in 2026/27 core spending power
findings.quote: For Oxford City Council, the settlement results in cash-terms zero increase in core spending power in 2026/27, which compares relatively favourably with several neighbouring districts though this still represents real-terms reduction once inflation is taken into account.

findings.headline: £32 million borrowing programme for housing acquisition to stabilise temporary accommodation costs
findings.detail: The budget sets aside £32 million for property acquisition, primarily through the Housing Revenue Account where borrowing is more affordable, as a strategic shift to reduce the council's exposure to rising temporary accommodation market costs.
findings.matters: This is a significant new borrowing commitment driven by inability to control TA costs through other means. It shifts the risk from annual rental volatility to long-term debt servicing.
findings.figures: £32 million
findings.quote: the budget sets aside £32 million, to reflect a strategic shift towards property acquisition, primarily through the Housing Revenue Account where borrowing is more affordable. This should reduce TA costs and limit the Council's exposure to costly TA markets, ultimately stabilising the spend over time.

findings.headline: Garden waste subscribers fell 10% despite 10% price rise; council at risk of revenue-reducing tipping point
findings.detail: Garden waste charging was increased 10% in 2025-26 but subscriber numbers fell 10% in the same period. The scrutiny group expressed concern about whether the council has reached a tipping point where further price increases are driving cancellations and undermining overall revenue. Oxford charges among the highest nationally for this service.
findings.matters: Loss of price elasticity is a warning sign. If further increases cause proportionally larger cancellations, revenue deteriorates despite higher charges — a compounding pressure.
findings.figures: 10% reduction in subscribers; 10% price increase in 2025-26
findings.quote: a 10% reduction in the number of garden waste subscribers has occurred alongside a 10% price increase in 2025-26. The Group asked whether the council has reached a tipping point at which further prices increases are driving cancellations thereby undermining overall revenue.

findings.headline: Parking income hit by congestion charge — city centre revenue down £80-100k per month after introduction
findings.detail: Following the recent introduction of a congestion charge, city centre car park ticket purchases have fallen by approximately 25%, while Park & Ride usage increased by 8%. Specific car parks show material declines: Oxpens typically generates £150k per month but fell to £67k in November; Worcester Street normally generates £200k per month but earned £130-150k in November. Officers note forecasting is challenging and updated projections are being developed for the February budget report, with potential draw on reserves if needed.
findings.matters: Parking revenue is budgeted income. A sustained 25% drop in city-centre usage is material and introduces significant forecast uncertainty just as the council is already planning to draw reserves.
findings.figures: Oxpens: £150k per month normal vs £67k November; Worcester Street: £200k per month normal vs £130-150k November; city centre tickets down ~25%; P&R usage up ~8%
findings.quote: Officers pointed out that preliminary figures suggested a significant reduction in income at some city centre car parks. For example, Oxpens typically generates around £150k per month, but income in November fell to approximately £67k. Worcester Street, which normally generate around £200k per month, was currently estimated to have earned between £130k and £150k for November.

findings.headline: Council drawing down up to £8 million in reserves over four-year MTFP to balance budget
findings.detail: The budget plan allows for use of up to £8 million in reserves over the full medium-term financial plan period. This use is described as necessary to keep the budget balanced in the short term but emphasised as unsustainable if continued indefinitely.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown indicates the council cannot balance recurring expenditure against recurring revenue, creating a structural deficit being masked by one-time resources. Depletion limits the buffer for volatility.
findings.figures: £8 million over MTFP period (2026-27 to 2029-30)
findings.quote: the MTFP allowing for use of up to £8 million over the term. However, while this enabled the budget to remain balanced in the short term, it was strongly emphasised that this would not be a sustainable position if continued indefinitely.

findings.headline: Finance Director retiring — Nigel Kennedy steps down after directing budget preparation
findings.detail: The Group Finance Director, Nigel Kennedy, who leads budget forecasts and financial analysis, is taking retirement after this budget cycle. This is noted as significant timing for the budget process.
findings.matters: A change in the finance leadership during a period of substantial uncertainty (LGR, funding cuts, volatile income streams) introduces transition risk and potential loss of institutional knowledge during a complex operational period.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: This year's Budget preparations are particularly poignant since they are the last ones that Nigel Kennedy will direct before he takes a well-earned retirement.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs already overrunning budget in year three, despite annual projections
findings.detail: By Q3 of the current year, spending on temporary accommodation was already approaching the full-year budget of £2.6 million, and officers acknowledged that on current trends a gross overspend is likely. The scrutiny group noted that historically budgets have underestimated this pressure. TA costs are heavily influenced by external factors like the economy and government policy, with small changes producing movements of hundreds of thousands of pounds.
findings.matters: TA is a volatile, growing liability that the council has repeatedly underbudgeted. Unchecked cost growth here is a structural pressure on the council's financial position.
findings.figures: £2.6 million full-year budget; approximately £500k rental income collected by mid-year suggesting ~£1m annually; £32 million allocated for property acquisition as mitigation
findings.quote: by the third quarter, spend was already approaching the full-year budget of £2.6 million. Officers acknowledged that, on current trends, a gross overspend is likely, though this may be partially mitigated by rental income and new TA stock coming on stream in the final quarter.

findings.headline: The council plans £489.43 million of new prudential borrowing over four years (£39.25 million General Fund, £450.18 million HRA), substantially increasing the debt burden.
findings.detail: This borrowing is to fund housing company loans, social housing, and operational capital schemes. The strategy notes this assumes 'full funding of the capital programme without the application of an optimism bias', meaning it is a baseline case, not a downside scenario. New borrowing brings Minimum Revenue Provision charges to the revenue account (except for loans to companies assumed to be repaid).
findings.matters: A lender needs to verify that new borrowing is affordable within the council's revenue budget and that the MRP charges do not destabilise reserves or force service cuts. The scale is material relative to a council the size of Oxford.
findings.figures: £489.43 million net prudential borrowing 2026/27–2029/30; £39.25 million General Fund, £450.18 million HRA.
findings.quote: There is approximately £489.43 million of net Prudential Borrowing anticipated from 2026/27 up to and including 2029/30. Of this, £39.25 million relates to General Fund financing and £450.18 million relates to HRA financing.

findings.headline: The council's property portfolio (£145.8 million book value) is coming under tenant stress from inflation and energy costs, and monitoring has shifted to shorter-term crisis management.
findings.detail: The council owns investment property with a gross book value of £145.8 million generating £11.02 million in annual rent (2024/25). The council reports that 'the focus has shifted to a shorter view because of the general economic pressures as a result of energy and inflation', and has implemented a tracker to monitor tenant arrears. This signals active tenant distress, not routine management.
findings.matters: A large property portfolio under tenant stress from energy/inflation is a leading indicator of rental decline and impairment risk. For a lender, it signals whether this income stream can be relied on to service debt or support capital projects.
findings.figures: Gross book value £145.8 million; rent receivable 2024/25 £11.02 million.
findings.quote: The focus has shifted to a shorter view because of the general economic pressures as a result of energy and inflation. A tracker has been implemented which considers current arrears positions and records a summary of the latest position and contacts with tenants.

findings.headline: The council acknowledges significant financial pressures in coming years and is shelving zero-carbon requirements in capital projects because they have become unaffordable.
findings.detail: The strategy states that inflationary pressures are making green building standards uneconomic for projects that do not generate income, and explicitly links this to 'significant financial pressures faced by the council in the coming years'. This is not routine cost pressure; it is forcing a retreat from stated policy due to affordability.
findings.matters: A council that cannot afford green commitments on capital projects is under real revenue stress. This signals tightening budgets and forced prioritisation, which affects both current spending and future service viability.
findings.figures: Projects costed assuming zero-carbon compliance but being built without it where 'budget is available'.
findings.quote: This is accentuated for projects that do not generate income. This is especially relevant given the significant financial pressures faced by the council in the coming years.

findings.headline: Available capital receipts have fallen sharply to £16.4 million, down from £40.9 million, because the council is running out of property to sell.
findings.detail: As of 31 March 2025, the council held £40.9 million in usable capital receipts but after financing capital spend, only £16.4 million remained. The council explicitly states it 'relied heavily' on capital receipts in the past but they are 'gradually being eroded' due to 'limited property available for sale'. This narrows the council's room to flex capital funding when pressures emerge.
findings.matters: Declining receipts reduce a council's ability to fund discretionary capital or respond to urgent need without borrowing. For a lender, it signals tightening financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £40.9 million in usable capital receipts as at 31 March 2025; £16.4 million available after financing.
findings.quote: In the past the Council has relied heavily on capital receipts to fund its General Fund Programme but with limited property available for sale these are gradually being eroded.

findings.headline: Oxford City Council will cease to exist on 1 April 2028 as part of local government reorganisation, cutting the four-year capital strategy in half.
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that from April 2028, it will cease to exist and its capital expenditure will become the responsibility of a successor authority. This is not a contingency—the strategy is written assuming this happens. For a lender, this means capital commitments made now run into an entity transition midway through the strategy period, raising questions about succession, debt responsibility, and project continuity.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether commitments survive the handover, who assumes the debt, and whether the successor authority has been defined or legally committed. This is not routine risk; it is fundamental structural change.
findings.figures: Four-year strategy to 2029/30; reorganisation date 1 April 2028.
findings.quote: if Local Government Reorganisation continues as expected, from 1st April 2028 Oxford City Council will cease to exist and the capital expenditure from that point onwards will be the responsibility of the successor

findings.headline: OCHL housing company dividend forecast to stop after 2026-27, with only £3m payable in that year and zero thereafter
findings.detail: The company dividend that was built into the MTFS is now forecast at only £3m for 2026-27 and then nothing. Shareholders were advised in December 2025 that future surpluses are dependent on planning permission for major schemes (Redbridge and Sandy Lane) which is not yet obtained.
findings.matters: A forecast revenue stream the budget depends on is evaporating. Future returns are now contingent on planning approvals that may not materialise.
findings.figures: £3m dividend 2026-27; £0 from 2027-28 onwards
findings.quote: After this year, there are currently no further dividends forecast by the Company or included within the councils MTFS.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves drawn down by £7.4m over four years to maintain balanced budget despite income pressures
findings.detail: The MTFS shows transfers from reserves totalling £7.4m over the four-year period. This represents ongoing structural use of reserves to balance the budget rather than sustainable income covering recurring costs.
findings.matters: Reserves are a finite buffer. Ongoing drawdown to balance recurring expenses signals the budget is not self-sustaining and reserves will deplete over time.
findings.figures: £7.4m reserve transfer over four years; £3.856m General Fund working balance maintained
findings.quote: Over the next 4 years the transfer from reserves is estimated at £7.4 million.

findings.headline: HRA peak debt rising to £800m by 2036-37 with interest cover ratio of only 1.25, leaving limited headroom for rate increases
findings.detail: The HRA business plan forecasts debt to peak at £800m. The annual interest cover ratio is approximately 1.25 throughout the plan period. A 1% increase in borrowing interest rates would add £1.5m in annual capital charges. Interest rate headroom is minimal.
findings.matters: HRA is borrowing heavily to fund housing development. Covenant headroom of 1.25x interest cover is tight and vulnerable to any rate increase or cost pressure.
findings.figures: £800m peak debt by 2036-37; 1.25 interest cover ratio; 1% rate rise = £1.5m additional annual charge
findings.quote: A 1% increase in borrowing interest rates could increase capital charges in the HRA by around £1.5 million per annum.

findings.headline: OXWED development partnership with £21m council loan outstanding produced £2.6m loss in 2024-25 and no return forecast for MTFS
findings.detail: The council's 50/50 partnership with Nuffield College at Oxpens has loaned £21m on a 4% above base-rate basis. The 2024-25 accounts show a £2.6m loss. Commercial land values have declined and whole-site returns have reduced substantially from October 2023 forecasts. The scheme is under masterplan review and unlikely to return cash to the council for four years.
findings.matters: A material capital investment is operating at a loss with no payback expected in the medium term. Further planning variations may be needed, adding time and uncertainty.
findings.figures: £21m outstanding loans; £2.6m 2024-25 loss; 4% above base-rate interest
findings.quote: It is unlikely that this strategy would lead to any financial return to the Council over the next 4 year MTFS.

findings.headline: Car park income reduced by £250k annually following Oxfordshire County Council's implementation of congestion charging
findings.detail: City centre car park income has fallen as a direct result of the county's congestion charge. The council has reduced car park income assumptions by £250k per annum for the forecast period as an early indication of the impact.
findings.matters: Income reduced by a decision made by another body outside the council's control. This represents ongoing revenue headwind unrelated to council performance.
findings.figures: £250k annual reduction over four years
findings.quote: Early indications are that the introduction of the congestion charging by Oxfordshire Council has seen some reduction in income from city centre car parks. An amount in the order of £250k per annum is considered prudent to reduce car parking by, in the light of this.

findings.headline: Legal services suffering significant staff turnover requiring £380k annual additional spend to replace locums with permanent staff
findings.detail: The legal team has experienced multiple staff departures that have proved difficult to fill on a permanent basis. The council is currently paying market rates for locum cover at significant cost. The proposed restructure adds £380k annually to move to permanent staffing, with only £200k offsettable from other lines.
findings.matters: Staff retention issues in core council functions signal HR/organisational problems. The restructure cost is a permanent recurring expense, not a one-off fix.
findings.figures: £380k per annum additional cost; £200k offset from elsewhere; £100k capitalizable; £1.9m current legal budget
findings.quote: The legal services team has of late suffered a significant number of staff losses which have proved difficult to replace on a permanent basis. Current vacancies are being filled by locums at significant cost to the Council.

findings.headline: Business rates income forecast to achieve zero growth above baseline for next four years, down from previous projections
findings.detail: The council previously forecast business rates growth above baseline. The MTFS now assumes no growth for the entire four-year period, a swing of £5.2m. The council is also in receipt of safety-net compensation of £1.3m in 2026-27, indicating baseline rates are under pressure from appeals.
findings.matters: A £5.2m income line that was expected to grow will now be flat. The need for safety-net payments signals business rate values are falling, not rising, in the council's area.
findings.figures: £5.2m reduction from forecast; £1.3m safety net payment 2026-27; levy rate 10% (down from 50%)
findings.quote: There is no growth above baseline forecast for the next 4 years, a reduction of £5.2 million to that previously forecast. Any growth above baseline is subject to levy payments of 10%, reduced from 50% previously.

findings.headline: Residents face 4.74% overall Council Tax rise; council identifies collection rate risk
findings.detail: While Oxford's own precept rises 2.99%, the average Band D Council Tax liability rises 4.74% overall due to Oxfordshire County Council's 4.99% increase and Police Commissioner's 5.30% increase. The council's risk assessment explicitly identifies 'the increased challenge of maintaining the collection rate' as a specific risk, suggesting concerns about resident ability to pay higher bills.
findings.matters: Collection rate decline directly threatens the council's revenue budget; higher bills increase the risk that residents will struggle to pay, affecting the council's financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Overall 4.74% rise; average Band D from £2,557.13 to £2,678.40 (£121.27 increase)
findings.quote: a risk relating to the increased challenge of maintaining the collection rate

findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report on Reserves and Balances
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will dissolve the council in April 2028; £2m allocated for preparations but 'lot of upfront costs' ahead
findings.detail: The council will cease to exist in its current form from 1 April 2028 when it becomes part of a Greater Oxford unitary authority. The budget includes £2m for LGR preparation work, but the report states there will be 'a lot of upfront costs to deliver the efficiencies' with timing and scale still uncertain pending government decision on unitary structure.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the council's medium-term financial plan extends beyond the organisation's existence. This creates unknown integration costs, uncertain service efficiencies, and potential for stranded assets or unfinished programmes.
findings.figures: £2m allocated for LGR preparation costs
findings.quote: The Council has included £2 million in its budget to commence work on preparations for LGR once the decision on the future direction of the Council is known in April 2026. There will be a lot of upfront costs to deliver the efficiencies and savings that we outlined in the Council bid to move to a Greater Oxford Council.

findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report on Reserves and Balances
findings.headline: Council relies on £12.6m of wholly owned company returns over MTFS, which the S151 Officer identifies as higher-risk income source
findings.detail: The council's budget depends on dividend returns from Oxford Direct Services and Oxford City Housing totalling approximately £12.6m over the four-year plan. The report explicitly states the 'Oxford Model' reliance on these income streams 'is more of a risk than simply reducing spend'.
findings.matters: The council is funding core services from commercial company profits rather than taxation or government grant. Any deterioration in company performance (as recently seen in OCHL) creates a direct budget shortfall rather than a controllable operational issue.
findings.figures: £12.6m in company returns forecast over MTFS
findings.quote: The Oxford Model's reliance on income streams from its wholly owned companies and other sources of income such as commercial rents (as illustrated below) to cover General Fund expenditure is more of a risk than simply reducing spend.

findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report on Reserves and Balances
findings.headline: HRA borrowing escalating to £651m with tight 1.25 interest cover ratio leaving no room for additional spend beyond 5 years
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account is planning to escalate borrowing from £270m to £651m to purchase affordable housing. This is controlled by an interest cover ratio of 1.25, which the report states leaves no flexibility for additional priorities beyond the next 5 years.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's overall debt position needs to understand the HRA's growing leverage and the tight constraint this places on future flexibility for maintenance, regulation compliance, or additional borrowing.
findings.figures: HRA debt increasing from £270m to £651m; interest cover ratio maintained at 1.25
findings.quote: At this level expenditure in the HRA both capital and revenue based on the estimates is affordable over the next 5 years although there is no room for any further spend over that period.

findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report on Reserves and Balances
findings.headline: Homelessness temporary accommodation costs could spiral by another £7m per annum without intervention
findings.detail: The council reports experiencing a significant increase in families and individuals placed in temporary accommodation. Without mitigation measures (principally purchase of 260 dwellings), costs could rise a further £7m annually. The success of the mitigation programme is critical.
findings.matters: Homelessness is an uncontrollable demand-led service with no natural cap. The council is hedging this with a housing purchase programme that itself requires sustained capital funding and adds to HRA borrowing.
findings.figures: Potential increase of £7m per annum in homelessness costs without mitigation
findings.quote: The Council estimate that without mitigation this could rise by another £7 million per annum. Mitigations include the purchase of 260 dwellings and this programme will need to stay on track if the mitigations to be successful.

findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report on Reserves and Balances
findings.headline: Business rates income lost £2-3m due to Finance Settlement reset removing all growth above baseline
findings.detail: The council's 85% share of business rates growth above baseline was eliminated by the Finance Settlement. This represents a direct cut to expected income despite the council holding one of the highest percentages of business rates growth in its comparator group.
findings.matters: A major income assumption in the council's model has been reset downward by government, requiring either efficiency gains to replace it or use of reserves. This reduces resilience for future resets.
findings.figures: £2-3 million loss of business rates income
findings.quote: The recent Finance Settlement has removed all growth above baseline with the Council losing £2million to £3million of business rates income as a result.

findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report on Reserves and Balances
findings.headline: Risk reserve being drawn down by £11.4m over MTFP, reducing financial buffer
findings.detail: The council has set aside £7.4m in its risk reserve to balance the 2026-27 budget, with a further £4m forecast to be drawn over the remainder of the four-year plan. This represents planned consumption of the financial cushion designed for unexpected problems.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's buffer for absorbing shocks is actively being consumed to fund core expenditure, not just held against contingencies. This reduces optionality in future years.
findings.figures: £7.4m risk reserve used to balance MTFP; £4m additional planned drawdown; total earmarked reserves falling from £56m to £45m
findings.quote: Within these reserves is also the 'risk reserve' £7.4 million which will be used to balance the MTFP, and a further £4 million of the risk reserve is forecast to be used over the life of the MTFP.

findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report on Reserves and Balances
findings.headline: 2025/26 budget already overspending by £1.3m, requiring draw from risk reserve
findings.detail: Budget monitoring to 31 December 2025 shows the council is tracking to an adverse variance of £1.3m even after budgeted transfers to reserves. This overspend is to be covered from the risk reserve held for exactly this purpose, consuming planned contingency early in the year.
findings.matters: An in-year overspend this early, and one that exhausts contingency reserves, signals that budget assumptions are proving optimistic and limits the council's ability to absorb further pressures in 2026/27.
findings.figures: £1.3 million adverse forecast outturn variance as at 31 December 2025
findings.quote: Budget monitoring for the 9 months ending 31 December 2025 indicates an adverse forecast outturn variance of £1.3 million after a budgeted transfer of £2.059 million to reserves. Should this position prevail then this will be covered from the risk reserve.

findings.headline: Service resilience at risk due to inadequate staffing in critical functions
findings.detail: Red service risk 00034 warns that service resilience is threatened by 'inadequate staffing and the requirement for expertise in response to major incidents,' and may 'necessitate increased reliance on external support or lead to operational delays.' This has 'direct impact on risk, compliance, expenditure, and income to the Council.'
findings.matters: Over-reliance on external/agency support drives costs up and can mask underlying service capacity problems. A lender would be concerned about hidden cost pressures from external staffing and the risk of service failure affecting income.
findings.figures: No specific figures given
findings.quote: inadequate staffing and the requirement for expertise in response to major incidents may necessitate increased reliance on external support or lead to operational delays

findings.headline: Service-level risk escalation: amber risks increased from 56 to 61 in one quarter
findings.detail: Service risk register shows amber risks rising from 56 in Q2 to 61 in Q3 (an increase of 5), while red service risks fell from 12 to 10. Over the same period, 4 new risks were added and 0 closed. This suggests growing service-level operational pressures that are not yet critical but deteriorating.
findings.matters: A trending increase in amber service risks indicates operational stress across the council and suggests conditions may worsen if pressures are not addressed. This is a leading indicator of potential budget control difficulties.
findings.figures: Service amber risks Q2: 56, Q3: 61; new risks added Q3: 4; closed: 0
findings.quote: The table below shows the number of service risks at 31 December 2025 compared with the previous reported quarters... Q2 2025/26 Q3 2025/26... Amber 56 61

findings.headline: Service-level legal services income target flagged as at-risk red risk
findings.detail: Service risk 00055 identifies a specific red risk: the Law, Governance and Strategy department's income target is not being achieved. If it continues to miss target, this 'will be placed on the overall legal services budget, leading to an overspend.'
findings.matters: Service-level budget pressures and unmet income targets indicate either over-optimistic forecasting or deteriorating income capacity. This pattern, if replicated across services, signals eroding budget flexibility.
findings.figures: No specific figures given
findings.quote: If the income target is not achieved, additional pressure will be placed on the overall legal services budget, leading to an overspend.

findings.headline: Commercial income streams depressed by economic conditions
findings.detail: The Financial Stability red risk identifies 'broader economic weaknesses, which may depress income streams such as commercial rents and business rates' as a key contributing factor to financial pressure. This acknowledges real vulnerability in the council's income base to wider economic conditions.
findings.matters: Commercial property income and business rates volatility directly impact the revenue budget and borrowing need. A lender would want to understand how exposed the council is to economic downturn and what income forecasting assumes.
findings.figures: No specific figures given
findings.quote: broader economic weaknesses, which may depress income streams such as commercial rents and business rates

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account under financial pressure and facing intensification
findings.detail: Risk 00105 flags the HRA as facing financial pressures that 'will intensify if the Council, as the local housing authority, fails to meet its housing prevention priorities for homelessness or deliver its Housing Revenue Account business plan and Asset Strategy priorities.' This is a red corporate risk ranked at the highest level.
findings.matters: The HRA is ring-fenced but its financial stability directly affects the council's overall financial position and borrowing capacity. Intensifying pressures could force service cuts, stock disposals, or require cross-subsidy from the general fund.
findings.figures: No specific figures given
findings.quote: ability to mitigate financial pressures within the Housing Revenue Account. These pressures will intensify if the Council, as the local housing authority, fails to meet its housing prevention priorities for homelessness

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs growing as homelessness demand rises
findings.detail: Multiple red risks flag temporary accommodation as a financial pressure. The council faces rising service demands for temporary accommodation, and faces potential failure to meet increasing homelessness demand or to implement cost control measures. Service-level risk 00109 explicitly warns of 'an increase in temporary accommodation costs' if prevention activities cannot meet sustained increases in homelessness.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a high-cost statutory obligation with volatile demand. Rising costs directly impact the council's revenue budget and borrowing requirements, and lenders track this as a key pressure point for councils.
findings.figures: No specific cost figures given
findings.quote: If, because of changes in Government policy, the Council's homeless prevention activities are unable to meet a sustained increase in homelessness, there will be a failure in service delivery and an increase in temporary accommodation costs.

findings.headline: Capital project costs escalating due to inflation
findings.detail: The Financial Stability red risk specifically identifies inflation-driven cost escalation affecting materials for capital projects as a key contributing factor to the council's broader financial pressures. This is undermining the council's ability to implement its plans amid increasing financial pressure.
findings.matters: A lender would need to understand whether capital schemes are at risk of budget overruns due to material cost inflation, and whether the council has mitigated this in project planning.
findings.figures: No specific figures given
findings.quote: inflation-driven cost escalation affecting materials for capital projects

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Corporate Risk Register Risk and Controls
findings.headline: Broad financial stability risk: pressure on income and increased demand could force service reductions and government intervention
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies risk of not being able to deliver its plans and corporate priorities due to pressure on income and increased demand for services. Causes include lack of knowledge on fairer funding, fluctuations in income/expenditure, inflation impacts, increased demand (including temp accommodation), and pressures on commercial operations (Oxford Model, OX Place needing business plan refresh at 2033 expiry).
findings.matters: This is the council's top-ranked financial stability risk (score 16). The outcome could include reduction in services, fee and charge increases, staff morale damage, and ultimately government intervention if pressures become unresolvable.
findings.figures: Risk score 16 (4 probability, 4 impact); OX Place business plan expires 2033
findings.quote: Pressure on income and increased demand for services means that the Council will not be able to deliver its plans and corporate priorities. Unresolvable pressures ultimately lead to government intervention.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Corporate Risk Register Risk and Controls
findings.headline: New Social Housing Regulation Act empowers unlimited fines for consumer standard breaches
findings.detail: The council now operates under a new regulatory regime (Social Housing Regulation Act) that gives regulators power to 'name and shame' underperforming landlords and issue unlimited fines. The council has completed a self-assessment and put a prioritised action plan in place, with new corporate Task Group oversight and resident/Member oversight to ensure progress across all four consumer standards areas.
findings.matters: Unlimited fine exposure is a material financial risk to the HRA. Non-compliance with consumer standards could result in significant unbudgeted costs and reputational damage.
findings.figures: Unlimited fines now possible under the new regime
findings.quote: The Social Housing (Regulation) Act has been provided with greater powers to "name and shame" underperforming local housing authorities as well as through its new inspection regime it will have the authority to issue unlimited fines to landlords.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Corporate Risk Register Risk and Controls
findings.headline: June 2025 cyber incident triggered 100+ security improvements now competing with BAU services for resources
findings.detail: A cyber incident occurred in June 2025, triggering an extensive security upgrade programme. Over 100 cyber security improvements have been identified and are being worked through, but the challenge is delivering these alongside business-as-usual services and existing projects with the same resource budget. Two interim resources were added but competing demands remain the biggest cause of delays.
findings.matters: A recent cyber incident is a material operational event; the large remediation backlog and resource constraints suggest the council's IT infrastructure remains at elevated risk during the recovery period.
findings.figures: Over 100 cyber security improvements identified; 75% of staff completed cyber security training as of December 2025
findings.quote: Over 100 cyber security improvements have been identified and ICT are working through these. The challenge remains that of having to deliver BAU services, projects, and the cyber improvements with the same resources.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Corporate Risk Register Risk and Controls
findings.headline: Sewage and energy infrastructure capacity constraints are limiting development growth and receiving ministerial oversight
findings.detail: Developers have identified lack of capacity in both energy and sewage treatment supply as risks to growth in both the short and long term. The Oxford Sewage Treatment Works is now one of only 20 projects nationally receiving regular ministerial oversight by the Environment Agency. The council is in quarterly discussions with utility providers and developers.
findings.matters: Infrastructure constraints directly cap the council's growth prospects and commercial income. Ministerial oversight signals a critical vulnerability that could delay or reduce development value.
findings.figures: Oxford Sewage Treatment Work is one of 20 projects receiving regular ministerial oversight
findings.quote: Lack of capacity of both energy and sewage treatment supply have been identified by developers as risks to growth in both the short and long term. The EA has confirmed that the Oxford Sewage Treatment Work is one of 20 projects receiving regular oversight at ministerial level.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Corporate Risk Register Risk and Controls
findings.headline: Legal department projecting overspend for 2025/26 due to unresolved retention crisis
findings.detail: Ongoing resource issues in the legal department are causing competitive pay disadvantages, leading to staff departures to less busy authorities. The council acknowledges these issues will be addressed as far as possible through restructure subject to overall funding constraints, but capacity continues to decline and risks increase.
findings.matters: A legal department overspend signals cash leakage from other priorities and reduced capacity to manage governance and compliance, both critical to council operations.
findings.figures: Projected overspend for 25/26
findings.quote: These will be addressed as far as possible in the restruture subject to overall Council funding. However they continue to increase in terms of reduction in capacity and risk with staff leaving due to competitive pay offers at less busy authorities. This is resulting in a projected overspend for 25/26.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Corporate Risk Register Risk and Controls
findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation placements surging with escalating costs to General Fund and HRA
findings.detail: The council's temporary accommodation stock has grown from 100 units to over 200, on track to reach 300 by December 2026. With this rapid growth comes increasing financial pressures on the General Fund due to rising placement costs. The council is now committing to purchasing 150 additional units as part of new mitigations agreed in May 2025, funded through the MTFP.
findings.matters: This is a direct, quantified drain on the council's budget with no clear end point, driven by external factors (cost of living crisis, housing shortage) the council cannot fully control.
findings.figures: Stock grown from 100 to over 200 now, on track to reach 300 by Dec 26; 150 additional units to be bought; 260 further units planned total
findings.quote: The Temporary Accommodation stock has grown from 100, to over 200 now, and on track to reach 300 by Dec 26, through leasing, HRA transfers, RP transfers, and over 55 decants.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Progress Report (Year ended 31 March 2025)
findings.headline: Auditors have identified a potential significant weakness in Value for Money relating to the council's capacity to support the audit
findings.detail: The auditors have flagged a potential VFM significant weakness specifically concerning the council's capacity to support the external audit process. This will be formally reported once the audit is completed.
findings.matters: A VFM significant weakness on audit support capacity is a governance red flag for lenders; it suggests the council may lack capacity to discharge other critical financial and operational responsibilities
findings.figures: One potential VFM significant weakness identified
findings.quote: We have identified one potential risk of significant weaknesses relating to the Council's capacity to support the external audit process.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Progress Report (Year ended 31 March 2025)
findings.headline: Quality of working papers is substandard and has triggered additional audit fees
findings.detail: The auditors found that working papers and supporting evidence provided by the council fell below audit standards, with complex calculations unexplained and third-party evidence missing. Management has agreed this will result in a scale fee variation.
findings.matters: Poor quality financial documentation increases audit risk and costs; it indicates weak internal controls and raises questions about the reliability of the underlying financial data
findings.figures: Scale fee variation to be raised (amount unspecified in this report)
findings.quote: The quality of the working papers and supporting evidence were generally below the standard required to support an efficient audit. This has resulted in an additional audit effort and therefore we expect to raise a scale fee variation in respect of this.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Progress Report (Year ended 31 March 2025)
findings.headline: Finance team capacity constraints have persisted for years and prevent timely delivery of financial statements and audit evidence
findings.detail: The council acknowledges multi-year capacity issues within the core finance team that have prevented delivery of financial information by statutory deadlines. These constraints continue to delay the current audit and prevent compliance with regulatory requirements.
findings.matters: Chronic finance team understaffing is a governance failure; it indicates the council cannot meet its statutory reporting obligations and raises questions about the reliability of all financial data
findings.figures: Issues ongoing since at least 2021/22
findings.quote: The Council has experienced capacity issues within the finance team for a number of years, which has impacted the ability to support the external audit process and complete this in an efficient manner by the target dates set by the Accounts and Audit (Amendment) Regulations.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Progress Report (Year ended 31 March 2025)
findings.headline: Auditors cannot obtain assurance over Property, Plant & Equipment and Investment Property valuations for the second consecutive year
findings.detail: The council has failed to provide sufficient supporting evidence for PPE and IP valuations. Auditors have agreed they will not obtain assurance over the closing balances of these material assets before the statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026.
findings.matters: PPE and IP are typically material balance sheet items; inability to verify valuations is a fundamental financial reporting failure that undermines credit quality assessment
findings.figures: Backstop date: 27 February 2026
findings.quote: Similar to the prior year, we have been unable to obtain sufficient supporting evidence for our sample selected for Property, Plant and Equipment (PPE) valuation testing and additions testing. Therefore, officers have agreed that we will not be in a position to obtain assurance over the closing balance of PPE in advance of the backstop date which is 27 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Progress Report (Year ended 31 March 2025)
findings.headline: Oxford has issued disclaimed audit opinions for three consecutive years due to inability to deliver timely financial statements and audit evidence
findings.detail: The council's 2021/22 audit was disclaimed, cascading into a disclaimer for 2022/23. The 2023/24 audit opinion was also disclaimed despite being signed on the last day of the deadline. This pattern reflects systemic capacity problems in the finance function.
findings.matters: Disclaimed audit opinions mean no independent assurance on the council's financial statements; three years running indicates the council cannot reliably report its position to creditors and regulators
findings.figures: Disclaimed opinions: 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24
findings.quote: The delays therefore resulted in a disclaimed audit opinion not only for 2021/22 but also resulted in a disclaimed audit opinion for 2022/23 as Council staff could not deliver to the required timeline in 2021/22. Similar issues were experienced during the 2023/24 audit with that audit being signed only on the last day before the backstop date and another disclaimed audit opinion was issued for 2023/24.

findings.headline: Multi-asset investment portfolio down 17.3% in value; property fund wind-down generating capital loss
findings.detail: The £5m Fidelity multi-asset fund has depreciated to £4.135m (17.3% loss) due to stock market falls driven by inflation and rising interest rates. Separately, the Lothbury property fund is being wound up with an expected total capital loss of £0.850m. Both continue paying dividends, and the Lothbury fund returned £1.460m more over its life than base-rate returns.
findings.matters: Demonstrates portfolio volatility and crystallised losses affecting reserve cover, though being actively managed
findings.figures: Fidelity £5m → £4.135m (£0.865m loss); Lothbury expected total loss £0.850m; Fidelity dividend 4.78% average return; Lothbury outperformed base rate by £1.460m over life
findings.quote: The capital value has fallen to £4.135m equating to a fall of (17.30) %

findings.headline: Statutory override protecting pooled fund investments from revenue impact ends in 2029, creating future earnings volatility
findings.detail: The government's statutory override that currently shields councils from revenue impact of pooled investment losses expires 31 March 2029. After that date, both surpluses and deficits on the council's £13.547m pooled funds and £14m National Homelessness Property Funds will flow through the revenue account. The council is holding an earmarked reserve against this risk.
findings.matters: Creates material uncertainty over usable reserves and revenue position in three years, directly affecting financial headroom
findings.figures: £13.547m pooled investment funds; £14m National Homelessness Property Funds; override expires 31 March 2029
findings.quote: Given the fluctuations in the property and money markets there is a risk of some adverse revenue impact when the override is removed and consequently the Council holds an earmarked reserve against this risk.

findings.headline: Council will require external borrowing to meet future capital expenditure
findings.detail: The council has avoided external General Fund borrowing by financing capital projects through internal cash resources. However, the report explicitly signals that external borrowing will be necessary in future to meet capital expenditure requirements. Currently all external debt (£288.526m) is Housing Revenue Account-related.
findings.matters: Marks a change from the current position and indicates future demand for credit market access, relevant to lender appetite and covenant headroom
findings.figures: £288.526m external borrowing (HRA-only); no General Fund external borrowing taken in last two years
findings.quote: However external borrowing will be necessary in the future to meet its capital expenditure requirements, and more external borrowing,.

findings.headline: HRA is ring-fenced with no general fund backup; the council explicitly warns of account collapse if balance is not maintained
findings.detail: The HRA must finance its activities entirely from the rental income it generates, with no access to general fund reserves. The report explicitly states that failure to maintain a positive balance would lead to HRA collapse at the council.
findings.matters: For a lender, this means there is no municipal safety net if the HRA encounters financial difficulty. The HRA must remain solvent through its own revenue alone.
findings.figures: Ring-fenced account with no general fund subsidy available
findings.quote: The HRA is a ring-fenced account and is required to finance its activities from the income it generates - predominantly rental income. Failure to maintain a positive balance of the HRA account would lead to the collapse of the HRA at Oxford City Council.

findings.headline: 63% of HRA tenants (5,115 of 8,077) depend on Housing Benefit or Universal Credit, creating policy risk to rental income
findings.detail: The HRA's rental income is highly dependent on government benefit policy. The majority of tenants rely on Housing Benefit or Universal Credit housing costs to pay rents. Changes to Local Housing Allowance rates or benefit eligibility would reduce HRA income independent of council action.
findings.matters: For a lender, this represents policy risk to revenue forecasts. Government decisions on benefit rates or caps could reduce HRA income materially and unpredictably.
findings.figures: 5,115 tenants claiming benefits as at end September 2025: 1,316 Housing Benefit, 3,799 Universal Credit; 63% of 8,077 total
findings.quote: As at the end of September 2025 there were a total of 5,115 HRA tenants (63%) claiming Housing Benefit or the Housing Cost element of Universal Credit

findings.headline: £4.024 million annual rental income is foregone on 98% of the existing stock due to rents being capped below formula rent
findings.detail: 7,986 of the HRA's 8,077 properties have rents below the formula rent that government policy prescribes. This arose from historical rent caps (2023/24 capped at 7% when CPI was 10.1%) and creates structural income loss that cannot easily be recovered as rents can only be moved toward formula rent on re-let following vacancy.
findings.matters: Unrecoverable foregone income weakens the HRA's revenue base and its ability to fund capital investment and maintain services without maximum annual increases.
findings.figures: 7,986 properties of 8,077 total; £4,024,020 annual rental income foregone; £77,385 weekly
findings.quote: Actual Rent is less than Formula Rent 7,986 £77,385 £4,024,020

findings.headline: Strategic review identified 10-year financial challenges requiring maximum rent increases to remain viable
findings.detail: External consultants conducting a 2024/25 HRA Strategic Review found that the HRA faces a challenging financial future within the next 10 years due to investment demands from new legislation and housing standards. The council states it needs to maximize income streams to remain viable and warns that a rent increase lower than inflation would create an unsustainable position with risk of failing tenants in service provision.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand if an HRA has structural financial problems ahead and whether rental income will be sufficient to fund obligations without general fund subsidy.
findings.figures: 10-year outlook; £4.024m annual rental income currently foregone on existing stock
findings.quote: A HRA Strategic Review undertaken by external consultants during 2024/25 identified that the HRA faced a challenging financial future within the next 10 years due to the scale of investment required because of the demands placed on it by new legislation and housing standards.

findings.paper_title: Q2 integrated performance report 2526 DRAFT v2.0
findings.headline: Blackbird Leys Regeneration site start delayed to October/November 2025 with completion now predicted for March 2027, pushing delivery 6+ months later
findings.detail: The GF element of this major regeneration project is forecast to slip by £0.19m in 2025/26. 'Anticipated date to start on site for shell and core now slipped to October/November 2025 with completion now predicted for March 2027.' This represents a material delay to a flagship capital project.
findings.matters: Major regeneration projects are bellwethers for a council's execution capability and often underpin economic development strategy. A 6+ month delay suggests either planning/approvals challenges or delivery partner issues. For housing-heavy councils, delays to major housing developments affect long-term borrowing assumptions.
findings.figures: £0.19m slippage for GF element of Blackbird Leys Regeneration; site start now October/November 2025, completion March 2027
findings.quote: Blackbird Leys Regenerations (GF element) - £0.19m slippage forecast for 2025/26. Anticipated date to start on site for shell and core now slipped to October/November 2025 with completion now predicted for March 2027

findings.paper_title: Q2 integrated performance report 2526 DRAFT v2.0
findings.headline: ODS Fleet Replacement Programme slipped by £1.744m (30% of budget) due to procurement delays, rolling into 2026/27 with no certainty on timing
findings.detail: The £1.744m slippage represents 30% of the budgeted fleet replacement spend. The report states 'A full review of the procurement process has delayed ordering new assets' and 'Much of the asset procurement is expected to roll over into 2026/27.' This is a material capital project with execution risk.
findings.matters: Fleet replacement is essential for service delivery (ODS is the council's parking and waste services company). A 30% slip suggests procurement challenges or market supply issues. For a lender, capital project slippages indicate execution risk and potential knock-on delays to other programmes.
findings.figures: £1.744m slippage (30% of ODS Fleet budget); forecast to roll into 2026/27
findings.quote: ODS Fleet Replacement Programme – a slippage of £1.744m (30% of the budget) is forecast. A full review of the procurement process has delayed ordering new assets and informed this latest forecast. Much of the asset procurement is expected to roll over into 2026/27

findings.paper_title: Q2 integrated performance report 2526 DRAFT v2.0
findings.headline: Revenue Service printing and postage costs overrunning by £0.250m despite decentralisation efforts, with no fix until 2026/27
findings.detail: Revenues and Benefits expected to overspend by £0.292m, of which £0.250k (actually £0.250m based on context) is from printing, postage and carriage costs for council tax and business rates billing. The council decentralised the printing budget from the corporate print room, but this 'insufficient to cover printing and postage costs', and reductions 'are planned although these savings will materialise from 2026-27 onwards'—a full year or more away.
findings.matters: This suggests a failed cost-control initiative; decentralisation was supposed to control costs but made them worse. The delay in fixing it (to 2026/27) means the council is absorbing a controllable overspend for a further year. It signals execution and procurement challenges.
findings.figures: £0.250m printing and postage overspend (revenues service); £0.292m total Revenues and Benefits adverse variance
findings.quote: Decentralisation of the printing and postage budget from corporate print room is insufficient to cover printing and postage costs for the Revenues Service. Reductions in printing costs associated with the annual billing of business rates and council tax are planned although these savings will materialise from 2026-27 onwards

findings.paper_title: Q2 integrated performance report 2526 DRAFT v2.0
findings.headline: Social Housing Regulation Act 2023 compliance has been elevated to a red corporate risk, explicitly identifying potential for major tenant safety incidents, regulatory intervention, and reputational damage
findings.detail: This risk was reclassified from amber in Q1 to red in Q2. The report states the risk 'evaluates the potential impact if the Council, in its capacity as a landlord, fails to fully comply with the Social Housing (Regulation) Act 2023 customer standards, particularly the Safety and Quality Consumer Standard', and notes that failure could result in 'a major incident that compromises tenant safety, leading to sanctions, regulatory intervention, and severe reputational damage.'
findings.matters: Regulatory intervention in housing is a serious reputational and operational threat. For a council that is a major landlord, regulator sanctions could constrain borrowing, trigger intervention, or require capital spending to remediate compliance failures. This moved from amber to red in one quarter, suggesting deterioration.
findings.figures: 1 red risk escalation in Q2 2025/26 (Social Housing Act); 6 red risks, 8 amber risks total
findings.quote: A failure to meet Social Housing (Regulation) Act 2023 customer/consumer standards – this risk has been reclassified from an amber risk in 1Q to a red risk in 2Q... Such a failure could result in a major incident that compromises tenant safety, leading to sanctions, regulatory intervention, and severe reputational damage

findings.paper_title: Q2 integrated performance report 2526 DRAFT v2.0
findings.headline: HRA housing acquisitions delayed, creating £0.264m shortfall in dwelling rent income year to date and £0.220m further pressure at year-end
findings.detail: The council's new home acquisitions—a core revenue driver for the HRA—are running behind schedule. Year-to-date, dwelling rent is underachieving by £0.264m specifically due to 'the timings of the acquisition of new homes', with a further £0.220m pressure forecast from 'delayed acquisitions' by year-end. This directly erodes the HRA's revenue position.
findings.matters: Rental income is fundamental to HRA stability and the council's housing strategy. Delays in acquisitions suggest either capital constraints or market challenges; either way, housing supply targets are slipping, which matters to lenders evaluating the council's ability to deliver its development programme.
findings.figures: £0.264m dwelling rent underachievement YTD from delayed acquisitions; £0.220m forecast pressure at year-end from delayed acquisitions
findings.quote: Dwelling rent underachieving by £0.264m due to the timings of the acquisition of new homes which generate rental income... pressures on dwelling rent of £0.220m arising from delayed acquisitions

findings.paper_title: Q2 integrated performance report 2526 DRAFT v2.0
findings.headline: Housing benefits expenditure forecast to overspend by £1.5m due to inability to claim subsidy on supported housing—a structural, uncontrollable cost
findings.detail: The council explicitly notes a £1.5m increase in net housing benefits costs expected at year-end, with supported housing benefit expenditure continuing to rise. The underlying problem is the council's inability to claim subsidy on supported housing accommodation benefit expenditure, and the council states it is 'actively working on mitigations' but acknowledges the situation is being 'monitored'—language suggesting no immediate fix exists.
findings.matters: Housing benefits are demand-driven and difficult to control; this cost is being borne by the council rather than funded through subsidy. For a lender, this signals uncontrollable expenditure growth driven by factors outside council management (homelessness, supported housing demand), a red flag for budget stability.
findings.figures: £1.5m increase in net cost of housing benefits; supported housing benefit expenditure continues to rise with no subsidy recovery available
findings.quote: current indications suggest that this will be offset by a £1.5m increase in the net cost of housing benefits payments as supported housing benefit expenditure continues to rise. The council is actively working on mitigations to try and contain overspends largely arising from the inability to claim subsidy on supported housing accommodation benefit expenditure

findings.paper_title: Q2 integrated performance report 2526 DRAFT v2.0
findings.headline: General Fund adverse variance of £0.641m is sticky and unchanged from Q1, with major pressures in staffing and support service costs
findings.detail: The adverse variance remains almost static compared to Q1's £0.656m forecast, indicating structural budget pressures rather than one-time items. Law, Governance & Strategy faces £0.462m adverse variance from staff recruitment difficulties and locum dependency; Financial Services £0.758m from salary cost pressures and revenue service printing costs; Information & Technology £0.7m including £0.5m cyber incident response.
findings.matters: Persistent overspends across multiple services suggest underlying cost control challenges, and repeated salary/staffing pressures indicate difficulty recruiting and retaining staff—a marker of operational stress in key support functions.
findings.figures: General Fund adverse variance £0.641m (Q1: £0.656m); Law/Governance £0.462m adverse; Financial Services £0.758m adverse; Information & Technology £0.7m adverse
findings.quote: The overall Net Budget Requirement for 2025/26 agreed by the Council in February 2025 was £30.25m... At 2Q there is an adverse projected 2025/26 outturn variance of £0.641m compared to the 2025/26 latest budget... almost static to the forecast adverse variance of £0.656m reported at 1Q

findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan provides for complete exhaustion of risk reserve to fund capital programme
findings.detail: The MTFP plans to exhaust the council's £6.690m risk reserve entirely and spend half of the £10.406m direct revenue funding reserve to finance the capital programme. This eliminates the council's contingency buffer for unexpected financial pressures.
findings.matters: Planned depletion of reserves to zero removes financial resilience for future shocks and limits capacity to respond to emergencies or changed circumstances.
findings.figures: Risk reserve £6.690m; direct funding reserve £10.406m
findings.quote: The current MTFP provides for exhausting the risk reserve and spending half of the direct funding reserve to fund capital

findings.headline: HRA repairs costs £7.82m over budget due to new Housing Regulator compliance standards
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account repairs overspent by £7.82m on £20.38m spend, driven by new compliance standards from the Housing Regulator requiring increased fire safety (£1.145m), asbestos clearance and surveys, and electrical upgrades on 5-year cycle (£0.724m). The council describes this as an "exceptional year" but has increased 2025/26 budgets to accommodate ongoing compliance costs.
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance costs are non-negotiable and recurring; budgets were insufficient and higher baseline spending will continue, reducing capacity for other investment.
findings.figures: £7.82m overspend; fire safety £1.145m; electrical upgrades £0.724m
findings.quote: The 2024/25 overspend for repairs is due to an exceptional year following the introduction of significant changes to the compliance standards set by the Housing Regulator. Notable areas in respect of this are Fire Safety, Asbestos and Electrical Upgrades / Inspections.

findings.headline: Housing benefit costs will increase from 1 April 2025 due to Universal Credit transfer, beyond council control
findings.detail: Housing benefit costs overspent by £1.491m in 2024/25. The council explicitly signals that working age claimants transferring to Universal Credit from 1 April 2025 will worsen this pressure. The council notes the service is largely commissioned outside its control by NHS, Oxfordshire County Council and other districts.
findings.matters: A policy-driven cost increase beyond the council's control is imminent, constraining the ability to manage this budget line in future years.
findings.figures: £1.491m overspend 2024/25
findings.quote: There will be an increased impact from 1 April 2025 as a result of working age housing benefit claimants being transferred to Universal Credit.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation overspend of £1.89m with £1.73m annual pressure embedded in forward budget
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation overspent by £1.89m in 2024/25 due to ongoing demand. The council has built a permanent £1.73m annual pressure into the 2025/26 budget and MTFP, indicating this demand is expected to persist as a structural cost.
findings.matters: Growing demand-led costs are difficult to control once embedded in budgets and signal housing market stress beyond the council's capacity to manage.
findings.figures: £1.89m overspend 2024/25; £1.73m annual structural pressure
findings.quote: Due to the ongoing TA demand the 2024-25 actual overspend is £1.89m. An annual pressure of £1.73m has been included in the base budget within the 2025-26 budget and ongoing MTFP to address the ongoing demand for this category of accommodation.

findings.headline: General Fund deficit of £1.549m requires transfer from risk reserve to balance
findings.detail: The council's operational spending exceeded revenue by £1.549m in 2024/25, forcing a drawdown from the risk reserve to balance the General Fund. This represents 5.4% of the council's £28.604m net budget requirement and signals the operating account is not covering costs.
findings.matters: Reserve transfers mask structural budget gaps and reduce financial flexibility for unexpected pressures in future years.
findings.figures: £1.549m deficit; £28.604m net budget requirement
findings.quote: deficit of £1.549 million ("m") before a recommended equivalent transfer from risk reserves required to balance the fund due to significant cost pressures such as Temporary Accommodation and net cost of housing benefit payments

news_drafts.headline: HRA debt affordability constrained by interest cover ratio of 1.25:1, with £450.2m borrowing planned
news_drafts.lead: HRA has no Minimum Revenue Provision requirement, so affordability depends entirely on rent income and business plan performance; a 1.25:1 interest cover ratio is tight and leaves no slack for adverse variances.

news_drafts.headline: Reserve balances forecast to decline, eliminating internal borrowing capacity and forcing external market reliance
news_drafts.lead: Loss of reserve cover forces the council into external borrowing markets for all future capital, increasing refinancing risk and exposure to market interest rates.

news_drafts.headline: Interest payable on debt to rise 84% from £18.2m to £33.4m annually over 4 years
news_drafts.lead: Interest costs are a fixed commitment that reduces budget flexibility; rapid growth signals deteriorating debt serviceability and rising revenue pressure.
